questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A mining company plans to start a coalmine close to a village and a stream. (a) Name the health risks that workers in such a mine face. (b) State what mining does to the water sources of the area and to its land and soil.

markingPoints.description: Names dust and noxious fumes as making miners vulnerable to pulmonary diseases
Names collapsing mine roofs, inundation and fires in coalmines as constant threats to miners
States that the water sources of the region get contaminated and that dumping of waste and slurry degrades land and soil and increases stream and river pollution

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Dust and noxious fumes make miners vulnerable to pulmonary diseases; collapsing mine roofs, inundation and fires in coalmines are a constant threat. (b) The region's water sources get contaminated, and dumping of waste and slurry degrades land and soil and increases stream and river pollution.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: The mineral resources department of a state has to explain to the public why its mineral deposits cannot last for ever, and what the state should do about it. (i) Give the reason why mineral deposits are not replaced as fast as they are used up. (ii) State what happens to the cost of extraction and to the quality of the ore as extraction continues. (iii) Suggest the steps the state should take to make its use of minerals planned and sustainable.

markingPoints.description: Explains that the geological processes of mineral formation are so slow that minerals required millions of years to be created and concentrated
States that the rates of replenishment are infinitely small compared with the present rates of consumption
States that costs increase as mineral extraction comes from greater depths
States that the quality of the ore decreases as extraction continues
Suggests planned and sustainable use, improved technologies to allow the use of low grade ores at low costs, and recycling of metals with scrap metals and other substitutes

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The geological processes of mineral formation are so slow, and minerals required millions of years to be created and concentrated, that the rates of replenishment are infinitely small compared with the present rates of consumption. (ii) Costs increase as mineral extraction comes from greater depths, and quality decreases. (iii) Use mineral resources in a planned and sustainable manner; evolve improved technologies to allow the use of low grade ores at low costs; recycle metals and use scrap metals and other substitutes.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
Ramesh's family has worked for years in the Koderma Gaya – Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand, lying on the northern edge of the Chota Nagpur plateau, where mica occurs as plates or leaves that split easily into sheets so thin that a thousand of them are layered into a sheet a few centimeters high. This mica is used in electric and electronic industries. Lately Ramesh has noticed that the miners fall ill with chest trouble, the wells near the mine no longer give clean water, and the fields around the village have turned hard and barren. He has also heard that the ore is now being taken from greater depths.

(a) Name the disease the miners around Ramesh's mine are vulnerable to, and the three risks that are a constant threat to workers in coalmines. (b) Ramesh finds the wells polluted and the fields hard and barren. Explain how mining is responsible for this, and name the two kinds of official safeguards that would help keep the damage under control.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) The dust and noxious fumes make miners vulnerable to pulmonary diseases; collapsing mine roofs, inundation and fires in coalmines are a constant threat. (b) Mining contaminates the region's water sources and, through dumping of waste and slurry, degrades land and soil and increases stream and river pollution. Stricter safety regulations and implementation of environmental laws check this damage.
